title: Malachra fasciata: How to Spot and Control It in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Malachra fasciata in Rice Fields: Identify and Control It
metaDescription: Malachra fasciata, or Bakembakem, has hairy stems and leaves cut into five lobes. Learn to spot it in rainfed palay and stop it before it seeds.
excerpt: Malachra fasciata is a hairy broadleaf weed that farmers call Bakembakem or lapnis na buluhan. It grows in rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. This page shows you how to spot it by its deeply cut, hand shaped leaves and white flowers, and how to control it before it drops seed.

heroImage.alt: Malachra fasciata, a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: Alexis López Hernández, CC BY, via iNaturalist

blocks.text:
This weed belongs to the mallow family, Malvaceae, the same family as okra and gumamela. Malachra fasciata has no widely used English name, so most people simply use its scientific name. In the bukid, farmers call it Bakembakem or lapnis na buluhan. Since it is a broadleaf weed, it is not a grass or a sedge.

You will see it in rainfed lowland rice fields. As an annual, each plant lives for one season and then dies. Seed is its only way to spread. When the plants flower and set seed, the seeds fall into the soil and wait for the next rains. That is how one missed plant can become a patch the next season.

Look for branched stems covered with yellowish hairs. The leaves are your best clue. Each one is cut deeply into 5 narrow lobes, spread out like the fingers of a hand. As a broadleaf weed, its leaves have netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. The flowers have white petals. Its close cousin, Malachra capitata, has shallowly lobed leaves and yellow petals, so leaf shape and flower color tell them apart.

items: Branched stems covered with yellowish hairs that you can see and feel.
Leaves cut deeply into 5 narrow lobes, spread like the fingers of a hand.
Flowers with white petals among the hairy leaves and stems.
Look alike tip: Malachra capitata has shallowly lobed leaves and yellow petals instead of white.
Netted veins on the leaf lobes, unlike the parallel veins of grasses and sedges.

blocks.text:
Malachra fasciata takes water, fertilizer and light that your palay needs. Its branched stems spread out and can shade young rice hills. The harm is greatest early in the season, while the rice is still small. In rainfed fields, where water can run short, the fight for moisture hurts even more.

Since it spreads only by seed, each plant left to flower adds to the weed seed in your soil. Some seed can also get mixed into the harvest and into palay you save for planting. Weeds like this can also give insect pests a place to hide. Its hairy stems make it unpleasant to pull by hand, so use gloves.

items: Wear gloves when you pull it, since the stems are covered with yellowish hairs.
Pull plants early, before the white flowers open, so no seed drops into the paddy.
Bring pulled plants out of the field and dry them away from the bunds, where seed could wash back in.
Keep shallow water in the field where your supply allows, since its seeds sprout on moist, exposed soil.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Malachra fasciata down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Malachra fasciata Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Malachra fasciata?

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Malachra fasciata

items.q: What is Malachra fasciata called in Tagalog or local names?
items.a: Farmers call it Bakembakem or lapnis na buluhan. It has no widely used English name, so people often use the scientific name instead. Names can differ between provinces, so check the plant itself. Look for stems with yellowish hairs, leaves cut into 5 narrow lobes, and white petals.

items.q: How do I control this weed in my rice field?
items.a: Start with clean seed and a well leveled field, and keep shallow water where you can. Hand weed early, with gloves on, before the white flowers open. If you need a herbicide, choose one for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label of the product.

items.q: How do I tell it apart from Malachra capitata?
items.a: Look at the leaves and the flowers. This weed has leaves cut deeply into 5 narrow lobes, and its petals are white. Malachra capitata has leaves that are only faintly lobed, with fine teeth, and its petals are yellow. Both have hairy, branched stems and grow in rainfed rice fields, so you can control them the same way.
